reasoning: Both sets share the same scaffolding: a single package, a Phase 0 interface task, spine/thicken/wiring/system phases, and context packets that mostly suffice. The deciding factor is the RL content. Set A specifies every environment precisely: rewards, starvation, the 11-value compact view, ball and fish speeds, catch radii, vision radii, and observation layouts down to field names. Its learning ladders teach the requested concepts: tabular Q-learning, then DQN, then a CNN for value learning; REINFORCE, then PPO, then school, then limited vision for policy gradients; fixed opponents, then naive co-learning, then opponent-pool self-play with cross-play for co-evolution. It adds ablations, a library-matching bar, and a statistically tested beat-random/beat-scripted claim for every rung. Set B never defines a reward signal for Snake, the fish or predator-prey, which is a real gap for a lab meant to teach reward shaping. B also moves predator-prey into a square arena, drops tabular learning, and leaves the replay viewer out of M1, so the first milestone can't show the user's 'watch a replay' success criterion. B does slice milestones more finely and its pipelines are cleaner (small entries, real minimal spines such as online Q-learning and REINFORCE standing in for PPO). But it has a leftover milestone (M3, 'check and explain the snake': reference plus write-up), M1 claims TRAIN-07 while WORLD-07 is deferred to M7, and its interface task freezes private pass-through hooks (guard, holm, apply_style, check_runs). A's weaknesses: each stage is one large milestone, PL-01 is a 16-row table that mixes constructors from every stage, and some framing is stale (the brief's 'Not doing: designing future environments now', and S2's 'deliberately revised shared core' after AD-09/AD-13 moved the revision ahead of M1). Overall, A is the more sound and complete plan.

strengths: Every environment is pinned down with numbers: rewards, speeds, radii, observation layouts as named field tuples
The learning ladders map directly onto the concepts the user wants (value vs policy gradient, exploration, partial observability, self-play), with ablations to show what each piece contributes
Statistically tested claims against random, scripted and library baselines, with a 90% library-matching bar
Contract types are complete code shapes with invariants and fixture cases; spine packets carry the frozen types they need
Clean stage-to-milestone dependency chain M1→M2→M3 with real dependency reasons
weaknesses: One very large milestone per stage instead of several vertical slices; M1 carries the whole Snake ladder, ablations, corridor and reference
PL-01's step table mixes constructors from all three stages, so it reads less like a call path
Stale framing: the brief's 'Not doing: designing future environments now', S2's 'deliberately revised shared core', and CORE-06's 'after the core's interface revision'
Long, dense spec and contract are heavy reading for a solo learner

strengths: Finer vertical milestone slicing (one fish → many fish → local sight)
Clean, short pipelines with real minimal spines (online Q-learning before DQN; REINFORCE before PPO)
Check-world gate (two-exit corridor, 1-D point) is a good guard against silent RL bugs
Write-ups, side-by-side checkpoint replays and the sight overlay serve the 'explain why it works' goal
